options.rationale: The same units can share one axis for a direct comparison.

options.text: `Monthly Price` in currency and `Runtime` in minutes
options.rationale: Different units need separate axes.

options.text: Target Hours and Actual Hours, both in hours
options.rationale: The same units make a shared axis easy to read.

options.text: Sales in dollars and a count of orders in hundreds
options.rationale: Dollars and counts have different units and scales.

explanation: A combined axis suits measures in the same units, because one shared axis allows a direct comparison. Measures with different units or scales belong on a dual axis.

stem: Target Hours and Actual Hours are both measured in hours. Why is a combined axis a better fit than an unsynchronized dual axis?

options.text: Both measures are read against one scale, so bar lengths can be compared directly
options.rationale: One shared axis removes any risk of two different ranges.

options.text: A combined axis lets the two measures use different mark types
options.rationale: Different mark types belong to a dual axis, which has a Marks card per measure.

options.text: A combined axis avoids needing `Measure Values` and `Measure Names`
options.rationale: Blending relies on exactly those two fields.

options.text: A dual axis cannot show two measures measured in the same units
options.rationale: A dual axis can show them, but the two axes might have different ranges.

explanation: With a dual axis each measure has its own axis, and the ranges can differ unless the axes are synchronized. A combined axis puts both measures on one scale, which suits measures in the same units.

stem: The analyst wants a dual axis, not a combined axis, for `Sessions (Count)` next to a measure already in the view. Where should they drop the `Sessions (Count)` pill?

options.text: On the existing axis
options.rationale: Dropping onto an existing axis blends the measures into one shared axis.

options.text: On Color on the Marks card
options.rationale: A measure on Color shades the marks; it adds no axis.

options.text: On the right side of the view, when a black dashed line appears
options.rationale: This creates a second axis on the opposite side.

options.text: On `Measure Names` in the Data pane
options.rationale: Dropping a measure there does not create an axis.

explanation: A second measure dropped on the right side of the view, at the black dashed line, becomes a second axis. Dropped on the existing axis, it would be blended instead.

stem: In a dual axis chart, minutes are drawn as bars. The analyst wants `Sessions (Count)` as a line and leaves minutes unchanged. Where do they change the mark type?

options.text: On the Marks card of `Sessions (Count)`
options.rationale: Each measure of a dual axis chart has its own Marks card and mark type.

options.text: On the All Marks card, which sets one type for every measure
options.rationale: That would change both measures to the same type, minutes included.

options.text: In the Synchronize Axis dialog
options.rationale: Synchronizing only aligns the ranges of the two axes.

options.text: On the `Measure Names` pill on Color
options.rationale: Color distinguishes marks and does not assign mark types.

explanation: A dual axis chart has a Marks card for each measure, so each can have its own mark type. Bars for one measure and a line for the other is the classic combo chart.

stem: What is the largest number of layered axes that a dual axis chart can have in Tableau?

options.text: Two, one on the left and one on the right
options.rationale: Two is the usual dual axis, but Tableau allows more.

options.text: Four, two on Columns and two on Rows
options.rationale: Tableau help states this limit.

options.text: Three, one for each of Rows, Columns and Color
options.rationale: Color is not an axis and has no layered axis.

options.text: Six, one for each of the measures in the Data pane
options.rationale: The number of layered axes is not tied to the measures available.

explanation: Tableau allows up to four layered axes: two on the Columns shelf and two on the Rows shelf. The common dual axis uses only two of them.

stem: The two axes of a dual axis chart show different ranges. Which two statements about Synchronize Axis are true? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: It is chosen by right-clicking the secondary axis
options.rationale: That is the documented way to start it.

options.text: It replaces the two measures with `Measure Values`
options.rationale: `Measure Values` appears when axes are blended, not when they are synchronized.

options.text: It gives both axes the same scale
options.rationale: The two axes then use the same range.

options.text: It is applied by dragging one measure onto the other axis
options.rationale: That gesture blends the measures into one axis.

options.text: It changes the second measure into a line
options.rationale: Mark types are set on the Marks cards, not by synchronizing.

explanation: The two axes of a dual axis chart are independent. Right-clicking the secondary axis and selecting Synchronize Axis puts both on the same scale.

stem: Which two statements describe a dual axis chart rather than a combined axis chart? (Choose 2 answers.)

options.text: The shelf keeps the two measures themselves
options.rationale: Measure Values is used only when axes are blended.

options.text: `Measure Names` on Color distinguishes the measures
options.rationale: That belongs to a combined axis chart.

options.text: Each measure has its own mark type
options.rationale: A Marks card exists for each measure.

options.text: A single axis is shared by both measures
options.rationale: A shared axis is what makes a combined axis.

options.text: It is created by dropping a measure onto an existing axis
options.rationale: That gesture blends the axes; a dual axis needs the right edge or the Dual Axis command.

explanation: A dual axis chart layers two measures, each with its own axis and Marks card, and it keeps the measures themselves on the shelf. A combined axis uses Measure Values and Measure Names instead.
